clue.text: The Belgian dog that swallowed a German admiral

blocks.clueFragment: The Belgian dog that swallowed a German admiral
blocks.note: surface: a dog that has eaten a naval officer
setter's reading: the breed's name has HIPPER, a German admiral of the First World War, sitting inside it

explanation.surface: A Belgian dog has swallowed a German admiral whole.
explanation.walkthrough: SC(HIPPER)KE: Admiral Franz von Hipper commanded German battlecruisers at Jutland, and his name sits inside the breed.
explanation.definitionFit: The schipperke is a small black Belgian breed, once kept as a watchdog on canal barges.

clue.text: Is this terrier ever the limit?

blocks.note: the saying goes that the sky's the limit, meaning there is no upper bound; the breed's name is pronounced the same as sky

explanation.surface: Someone exasperated asks whether a particular terrier is ever too much to bear.
explanation.walkthrough: No indicator is printed: the solver must hear 'the Skye's the limit' in the old saying. Skye is a Hebridean island off Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Skye terrier is a long-coated Scottish breed named after the island where it was developed.

clue.text: Lone whale (anag.)

definitions.note: an early clue with no separate definition: the whole clue simply points to the rearranged word

indicators.note: an old-style abbreviation telling the solver outright that the preceding words must be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written: nine letters of fodder

explanation.walkthrough: An early-style clue with no definition at all: the solver simply rearranges the two words to the festival of 31 October.
explanation.definitionFit: No definition is given; the rearranged letters spell the name of the eve of All Saints' Day.

clue.text: Puttin' em in pigtails, 14 lady? It sounds like it

indicators.note: the setter says outright that the phrase is to be heard, so its pronunciation counts, not its spelling

blocks.note: putting hair into pigtails is plaiting it, and the clipped 'plaitin' 'em' is said like the precious metal
14 is FAIR-HAIRED, and a fair-haired lady is a blonde

explanation.surface: A colloquial line about plaiting a fair-haired woman's hair into pigtails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plaitin' 'em' said quickly sounds like PLATINUM; the 14 cross-reference, FAIR-HAIRED, turns 'lady' into a blonde.
explanation.definitionFit: A platinum blonde is a woman with very pale silvery fair hair, so she is a fair-haired lady.

clue.text: " Beauty's — yet is crimson in they lips " (Romeo)

blocks.clueFragment: " Beauty's — yet is crimson in they lips "
blocks.note: surface: a line of verse with a word missing, about red lips
setter's reading: the speaker is Romeo in Juliet's tomb, so the gap is filled from that speech, where beauty's flag still flies

explanation.surface: Romeo gazes at Juliet in the tomb and sees that her lips are still red.
explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation: Romeo says death has not conquered her, for beauty's ENSIGN, its flag, still flies crimson in her lips.
explanation.definitionFit: An ensign is a flag or banner, and Romeo imagines beauty flying its red colours on Juliet's lips.

clue.text: Sometimes hardly dressed in dusters

blocks.note: surface: someone barely clothed, wrapped only in cleaning cloths
setter's reading: brass knuckle-dusters, worn over the finger joints, which are hard

explanation.surface: Someone scantily clad, wearing nothing but dusters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardly dressed' means barely clothed in the surface, but here it means dressed in something hard: the brass of a knuckle-duster.
explanation.definitionFit: Knuckles are the finger joints that a knuckle-duster, a metal weapon, is slipped over.

clue.text: Lytton's learned murderer

blocks.note: surface: a scholarly killer belonging to someone called Lytton
setter's reading: Edward Bulwer-Lytton's 1832 novel about Eugene, a schoolmaster who killed a man

explanation.walkthrough: Eugene Aram was a real eighteenth-century schoolmaster and philologist hanged for murder; Bulwer-Lytton made him the hero of a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Bulwer-Lytton's novel Eugene Aram tells of a gentle scholar who turns out to have committed a murder.

clue.text: Cheer up, eel-catchers: there's money in it

indicators.note: 'there's money in it' says the thing wanted lies inside the preceding words

blocks.note: the letters run across cheer, up and eel
surface padding that turns the eel into a fishing scene

explanation.surface: Someone cheers on eel fishermen, assuring them their catch will pay.
explanation.definitionFit: The rupee is the currency unit of India and several neighbouring countries.

clue.text: This beak's point is not quite in the middle

blocks.clueFragment: This beak's point is not quite in the middle
blocks.note: surface: a bird's bill whose tip is off-centre

blocks.clueFragment: point is not quite in the middle
blocks.note: setter's reading: the word 'is' sits just short of the centre of the ten-letter answer

explanation.surface: A bird's bill grows slightly lopsided, its tip off-centre.
explanation.walkthrough: Beak is British slang for a magistrate. In MAG-IS-TRATE the letters IS are fourth and fifth, just off the middle of ten.
explanation.definitionFit: Beak is old British slang for a judge or justice of the peace who hears minor cases.

clue.text: The sort of part that could never cause a blush?

blocks.clueFragment: The sort of part that could never cause a blush?
blocks.note: surface: a decent, respectable role or bit that would not embarrass anyone
setter's reading: a part of a whole in arithmetic, less than one, which mathematicians call proper rather than improper

explanation.surface: An actor wonders which role is so respectable it could never embarrass.
explanation.walkthrough: In arithmetic a fraction less than one, like 3/4, is proper; one greater, like 5/4, is improper, and only impropriety makes anyone blush.
explanation.definitionFit: A fraction is a part of a whole, and one with numerator smaller than denominator is called proper.

clue.text: Lay back at round conference

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the word is read from its end
turning something round faces it the other way, so this little word is read backwards too

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sat back during a round-table meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: Both words are turned: LAY becomes YAL and AT becomes TA.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1945 Yalta Conference in Crimea saw Churchill, Roosevelt and Stalin plan postwar Europe.

clue.text: Should seek fresh employment if in a 26

definitions.text: Should seek fresh employment if in a 26

blocks.clueFragment: Should seek fresh employment if in a 26
blocks.note: surface: someone in the wrong job ought to look for another
setter's reading: 26 completes the idiom for a misfit, an object of one shape jammed into an opening of another

explanation.surface: Careers advice: anyone stuck in an unsuitable post should look for a new one.
explanation.walkthrough: Together with 26 this makes 'a square peg in a round hole', the idiom for a person unsuited to their position.
explanation.definitionFit: A square peg is a misfit, someone whose talents do not match the role they occupy.

clue.text: Surrey town, of ill omen to the monarchy?

blocks.note: woe, misfortune, in its old spelling wo
a king heads a monarchy

explanation.surface: A commuter town in Surrey is supposedly unlucky for the royal family.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as 'Wo, king!', a cry of woe to a king. Surrey is a county just south-west of London; Woking is a commuter town there.
explanation.definitionFit: Woking is a large town in north-west Surrey, on the main railway line into London.

clue.text: Perhaps some good osteopath could effect an improvement in these smoker's products!

blocks.clueFragment: Perhaps some good osteopath could effect an improvement in these smoker's products!
blocks.note: surface: a bone specialist treating the ailments of tobacco users
setter's reading: the smoker is a smokehouse curing fish, which are split and flattened along a backbone an osteopath might straighten

explanation.surface: A joke that heavy smokers are so crooked they need a bone-setter.
explanation.walkthrough: A smoker here is a fish-curer's smokehouse, not a tobacco user; its split, flattened herrings have backbones crying out for an osteopath.
explanation.definitionFit: Kippers are herrings split open, salted and cold-smoked, a traditional British breakfast fish.

clue.text: Olaf is more likely to be than Giuseppe

definitions.text: Olaf is more likely to be than Giuseppe

blocks.clueFragment: Olaf is more likely to be than Giuseppe
blocks.note: surface: a comparison of two men, a Scandinavian and an Italian
setter's reading: the typical Norseman has light-coloured hair, unlike the typical dark Italian

explanation.surface: Two men compared: one Scandinavian, one Italian, and which is likelier to be something.
explanation.walkthrough: Olaf is a typical Norwegian name and Giuseppe a typical Italian one; the stereotype is the pale Scandinavian against the dark Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair-haired means having blond or light hair, the colouring popularly associated with Scandinavians.

clue.text: A meeting place—for explorers?

definitions.note: the answer is the thing explorers use, a route or line of approach

blocks.note: taken as written
a venue is where an event or meeting is held

explanation.surface: Somewhere explorers might gather before setting off.
explanation.walkthrough: Explorers open up new avenues, whether of travel or inquiry; the dash separates the charade from that loose definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An avenue is a route or approach, as in an avenue of inquiry that researchers follow.

clue.text: He may investigate the declarer's bona fides

definitions.text: He may investigate the declarer's bona fides

blocks.clueFragment: He may investigate the declarer's bona fides
blocks.note: surface: someone checking whether a person making a statement is genuine
setter's reading: a traveller declaring goods at customs, whose luggage an official goes through

explanation.surface: An investigator checks whether someone making a declaration is honest.
explanation.walkthrough: The declarer sounds like a bridge player or witness, but this is the traveller at customs, and the official who rummages through bags is a customs searcher.
explanation.definitionFit: A searcher is one who looks through things, and a customs searcher examines travellers' baggage for undeclared goods.

clue.text: Oaks or Houyhnhnms, for instance

definitions.note: a single named event standing for the answer
a whole people standing for the answer

blocks.note: first meaning: the Oaks is a classic flat race for fillies run at Epsom
second meaning: the rational talking horses of Gulliver's Travels, a race of horses

explanation.surface: Two odd examples, trees and Swift's horse-people, offered as instances of something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oaks' looks like trees, but it is the Epsom fillies' race; Swift's Houyhnhnms are a race in the other sense, a people made of horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A race among horses is a contest at a course; a race of horses is a whole people of them.

clue.text: Disturbed soul-life of spirits

definitions.note: the answer is a by-product of distilled spirits, so 'of spirits' describes it rather than naming it

indicators.note: something disturbed has been thrown out of its settled order, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, eight letters

explanation.surface: A troubled inner life of ghosts or of the spirit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spirits' points at ghosts or souls, but these are distilled alcoholic drinks.
explanation.definitionFit: Fusel oil is a mixture of heavier alcohols formed in fermentation, found in poorly distilled liquor.

clue.text: A mechanical baby is one, but a real baby can't

blocks.clueFragment: A mechanical baby is one, but a real baby can't
blocks.note: surface: a wind-up toy infant can do something a real infant cannot
setter's reading: a small car, a baby of the motor trade; a real infant is too young to dash around

explanation.surface: A clockwork doll can do something a real infant cannot.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'baby' car such as the Austin Seven was a small runabout; a real baby cannot yet run about.
explanation.definitionFit: A runabout is a small light car for short local trips, the kind once nicknamed a baby car.

clue.text: Mount that was reversed to start a popular song

indicators.note: reversed means turned the other way round, so the letters are read from last to first

blocks.note: the music-hall song 'Ta-ra-ra Boom-de-ay' starts with these syllables

explanation.surface: A mountain once turned around to open a well-known tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ta-ra-ra Boom-de-ay' was an 1890s music-hall hit. The six letters read the same as the mountain backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Ararat is the mountain in eastern Turkey where Noah's ark is said to have come to rest.

clue.text: Calmness

blocks.note: surface: a plain word for serenity, which seems to want a simple synonym
setter's reading: an old word for the humour said to make a person sluggish and unexcitable, which is also mucus

explanation.walkthrough: A one-word definition: the less common sense of the answer is placid self-possession, from the medieval humour once blamed for a sluggish temperament.
explanation.definitionFit: Phlegm also means composure or imperturbability, from the old belief that a phlegmatic humour made people unexcitable.

clue.text: Saintly jazz expert

definitions.note: adjective; the answer is the name of a saint

blocks.note: first meaning: St ..., fourth-century bishop of Milan
second meaning: Bert ..., the popular British dance-band leader of the 1930s

explanation.surface: A jazz authority with a saint-like character.
explanation.walkthrough: Bert Ambrose led one of Britain's best-known dance bands, broadcasting from London hotels between the wars.
explanation.definitionFit: St Ambrose was the bishop of Milan who baptised Augustine; Bert Ambrose was a celebrated British bandleader.

clue.text: You don't say you will be unless you're pretty certain

definitions.text: You don't say you will be unless you're pretty certain

blocks.clueFragment: You don't say you will be unless you're pretty certain
blocks.note: surface: advice not to promise anything you are unsure of
setter's reading: the phrase 'I'm ... to', meaning something is sure to happen

explanation.surface: A piece of advice: never commit to something unless you are confident of it.
explanation.walkthrough: You only say you are bound to do something when you are sure of it; the clue reads like a moral but defines the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Bound means certain or destined, as in 'it's bound to rain', or obliged by a promise.

clue.text: In which bullying is quite justifiable

definitions.text: In which bullying is quite justifiable

blocks.clueFragment: In which bullying is quite justifiable
blocks.note: surface: a setting where intimidating others is allowed
setter's reading: the bully-off, two players clashing sticks to start or restart play in a field game

explanation.surface: A place where intimidation is perfectly acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: In field hockey, play once began with a bully-off, two players tapping sticks together over the ball, so bullying is part of the rules.
explanation.definitionFit: Hockey is the stick-and-ball team game whose traditional restart was called the bully.

clue.text: His feminine counterpart from N.Y was " the subject of all the Town's talk "

blocks.clueFragment: His feminine counterpart from N.Y was " the subject of all the Town's talk "
blocks.note: surface: a man whose female equivalent from New York was the talk of society
setter's reading: the man is a dandy or admirer whose female counterpart is a belle, the toast of the town

explanation.surface: A man whose female equivalent from New York became the talk of the town.
explanation.walkthrough: Beau and belle are the male and female forms of the French for beautiful; a belle is the reigning beauty everyone talks about.
explanation.definitionFit: A beau is a dandy or a woman's admirer, the male match for the belle of society.

clue.text: See 11

blocks.note: surface: a cross-reference sending the solver to another clue
setter's reading: this is the second half of the idiom begun at 11, the opening the misfit is jammed into

explanation.walkthrough: Clued only through 11: a square peg in a round hole is the person in the wrong job.
explanation.definitionFit: In the idiom about a misfit, the circular opening is where an awkwardly shaped piece will never sit properly.

clue.text: Likeness, as Father Time might say

blocks.note: speaking of himself, the figure would begin 'I am', contracted
Time personified is the passing of years, so he would call himself by that

explanation.surface: A likeness of the old man with the scythe.
explanation.walkthrough: Father Time, the bearded figure with scythe and hourglass, might introduce himself: 'I'm age'.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a likeness or representation, such as a portrait or reflection of someone.

clue.text: Said " Everybody has won, and all must have prizes "

blocks.clueFragment: Said " Everybody has won, and all must have prizes "
blocks.note: surface: an unnamed speaker declaring that no one lost

blocks.clueFragment: " Everybody has won, and all must have prizes "
blocks.note: setter's reading: the verdict after the Caucus-race in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, given by an extinct bird

explanation.walkthrough: In Alice in Wonderland the animals run a pointless Caucus-race and the Dodo declares everyone a winner.
explanation.definitionFit: The dodo, an extinct flightless bird of Mauritius, appears as a character in Lewis Carroll's Wonderland.

clue.text: Most of this Tiger is a literary Dane

blocks.clueFragment: Most of this Tiger is a literary Dane
blocks.note: surface: a big cat that is mostly Danish
setter's reading: the novelist and playwright Clemence Dane, whose first name takes up all but the last two letters

explanation.surface: A tiger that turns out to be mostly a Danish writer.
explanation.walkthrough: Georges Clemenceau, French premier in the First World War, was nicknamed 'the Tiger'; CLEMENCE is the pen name of the English writer Clemence Dane.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tiger was the nickname of Georges Clemenceau, the fierce French prime minister of 1917 to 1920.
